<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S4.SS2" title="In 4 Experiments ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4.2 </span>RQ1: High-Fidelity Performance Estimation</span></a></li>

</ol></li>

<div class="ltx_authors">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The paradigm of scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) in both parameter size and test time has pushed the boundaries of AI capabilities, but at the cost of making the traditional generative evaluation paradigm prohibitively expensive, therefore making the latency of LLM’s in-training downstream performance evaluation unbearable. However, simple metrics like training loss (perplexity) are not always correlated with downstream performance, as sometimes their trends diverge from the actual task outcomes. This dilemma calls for a method that is computationally efficient and sufficiently accurate in measuring model capabilities.
To address this challenge, we introduce a new in-training evaluation paradigm that uses a lightweight probe for monitoring downstream performance. The probes take the internal representations of LLM checkpoints (during training) as input and directly predict the checkpoint’s performance on downstream tasks measured by <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">success probability</em> (i.e., pass@1). We design several probe architectures, validating their effectiveness using the OLMo3-7B’s checkpoints across a diverse set of downstream tasks. The probes can accurately predict a checkpoint’s performance (with avg. AUROC<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math>0.75), have decent generalizability across checkpoints (earlier predicts later), and reduce the computation latency from <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1 hr (using conventional generative evaluation method) to <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>3 min. In sum, this work presents a practical and scalable in-training downstream evaluation paradigm, enabling a more agile, informed, and efficient LLM development process.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With the continuous scaling of model parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, the engineering behind training Large Language Models (LLMs) has become increasingly complex, necessitating auxiliary mechanisms for in-training supervision. Unlike traditional supervision that prioritizes training stability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chowdhery et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, capability-oriented in-training evaluation focuses on verifying whether the capabilities acquired by the model align with expectations for each downstream task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Groeneveld et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This approach involves tracking evaluation metrics across various downstream tasks rather than relying solely on training perplexity (PPL, i.e., loss). When detecting performance deviations in a specific task, researchers can intervene by adjusting data mixtures to rebalance the model’s overall competence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Crucially, perplexity metrics lack this granularity–while perplexity tends to plateau after convergence, performance on downstream tasks often continues to evolve as training progresses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As the capability boundaries of LLMs expand, the paradigm of in-training evaluation is shifting from traditional formats (e.g., multiple-choice) toward generative evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Myrzakhan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This transition is driven by the predominance of generative demands in modern downstream tasks; generative evaluation not only better reflects LLM’s generalizability, but also assesses LLM’s ability to handle increasingly complex problems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2022b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bubeck et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
However, this expansion aligns with the evolution of scaling laws: while previous scaling focused on parameter count and training data size, recent trends emphasize test-time scaling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Snell et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This shift not only escalates the computational cost of a single forward but also significantly increases the token consumption required for generative evaluation.
The resulting latency poses a severe bottleneck: for instance, if running a full evaluation on a benchmark takes tens of hours, low-latency in-training monitoring becomes computationally prohibitive and practically infeasible.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.01025v1/main.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/243;" width="429" height="243" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Workflow comparison between the current generative evaluation paradigm and the proposed probing evaluation paradigm for in-training downstream monitoring. Current paradigm suffers from high evaluation cost and excessive latency, resulting in delayed feedback to training progress. In contrast, probe can bypasses the generation process during the evaluation phase, thereby enabling rapid and timely assessment.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For the reasons outlined above, perplexity remains an inadequate surrogate to serve as a reliable proxy for downstream performance. While engineering solutions attempt to reduce evaluation latency by sampling a small-enough subset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Polo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, this approach inevitably introduces estimation bias <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Myrzakhan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Consequently, there is an urgent requirement for a new in-training evaluation paradigm that is both accurate and low-latency. To address this challenge, we introduce an efficient probe evaluation framework that utilizes a probe model to monitor downstream performance. The probe model takes the internal states of the model under training and the task input text as inputs, and predicts the corresponding performance metrics (e.g., accuracy and pass@k). Crucially, this allows us to bypass the computationally expensive generation, directly yielding performance predictions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate several probe architectures, specifically the LoRA-based probe and submodel-based probe, evaluate their performance against some simple baselines. These experiments are conducted under a generative evaluation framework across diverse domains, including general tasks, mathematics, and code generation. The results demonstrate that our method maintains high predictive fidelity (AUROC <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&gt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&gt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&gt;</annotation></semantics></math> 0.75) while drastically reducing evaluation latency, slashing the time required from <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1 hour to <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>3 minutes (on OLMo3-7B-base). Consequently, our framework revitalizes the possibility of low-latency, lightweight in-training evaluation once again in the era of modern LLM training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.01025v1/method.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/229;" width="381" height="229" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S1.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Demonstration of the working process of in-training downstream performance evaluation framework in training stage, and the structure of two lightweight probe models. Training would be applied only in specific checkpoints. Once a probe is trained, it could maintain predictability in the future checkpoints.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our main contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">❶</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a novel framework for efficiently in-training downstream evaluation by leveraging lightweight probe models. The proposed method can give feedback accurately with a low latency.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">❷</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design and evaluate three distinct probe architectures (submodel and LoRA) to predict task-specific success probabilities from the model’s internal states.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.ix3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">❸</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We empirically demonstrate on diverse domains that our trained probes exhibit strong cross-checkpoint generalization, enabling accurate performance prediction for future training steps.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.ix4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">❹</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.ix4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.ix4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our method provides a practical, low-latency workflow to the current in-training evaluation paradigm, enabling a more agile and informed LLM training process.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Works</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Predictability AI</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2025)</a></cite> introduces the fundamental idea of predictable AI that an AI system’s key validity indicators can be anticipated (e.g., performance). <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schellaert et al. (2025)</a></cite> further analyse the predictability of whether the performance of LLM is predictable. Therefore, many works have attempted to better predict the downstream performance of an LLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The most popular approach is to train a third-party model for performance prediction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pacchiardi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, while another approach predicts the task-level performance directly rather than individual-level performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These works make efforts on LLMs’ performance prediction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM In-training Supervision</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A vast array of intrinsic metrics inside LLM are proposed to either monitor or stabilize the training process. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al. (2023)</a></cite> explores the rank collapse inside the attention mechanism and uses the relative norm to measure such collapse. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team (2025)</a></cite> discovers the explosion of “MaxLogit” and proposes to stabilize training using QK-Clip. Some works find that the massive values inside attention are crucial for contextual understanding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, while others also find that a stable training process is also related to a stable behavior of attention entropy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Besides in-training monitoring, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2025)</a></cite> produces a new perspective for in-training evaluation by building the correlation between the loss value and downstream performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Probe</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work suggests there is a “truthfulness” direction in latent space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marks and Tegmark, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Azaria and Mitchell, 2023</a>)</cite>. Some studies employ linear probes to predict whether a model’s answers are correct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. To reduce reliance on the model’s generated responses and speed up prediction, certain approaches directly feed the question’s hidden state into the probe to assess the model’s ability to provide accurate answers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Snyder et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gottesman and Geva, 2024</a>)</cite>. However, correctness and factuality are not entirely linearly encoded <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wehner et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Therefore, this work proposes the sub-model probe, which captures the dynamic flow of information within the model to predict its performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methods</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The primary objective of in-training probe evaluation is to develop a framework for rapidly and efficiently estimating an LLM’s performance on downstream tasks without resorting to computationally expensive full-scale evaluations. To achieve this, we first model the generative evaluation process (from input text to generation, then gathering the results to obtain the Pass@1 score) as a regression task, and then introduce a lightweight probe to approximate it.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preliminaries: Performance Estimation as Value Approximation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The evaluation process can be modeled as value approximation. Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> denote a large language model parameterized by weights <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. Given a prompt <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> from the dataset <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, the model generates a response <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> following the policy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}(y|x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}(y|x)</annotation></semantics></math>.
To quantify the performance, we define a ground-truth reward function <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(x,y)\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(x,y)\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>, which evaluates whether the response <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> correctly solves the problem in the prompt <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. Our goal is to estimate the expected performance of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> on a downstream task without performing a full-scale evaluation.
Adopting a reinforcement learning (RL) perspective, we treat the prompt <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> as the state <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\in\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\in\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and the generated response <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> as the action <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a\in\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\in\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>. The performance of the model on a specific prompt can be modeled as the state-value function <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{\pi}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{\pi}(s)</annotation></semantics></math>, which represents the expected reward under the current policy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s)}[Q^{\pi}(s,a)]=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{\theta}(a|s)Q^{\pi}(s,a)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s)}[Q^{\pi}(s,a)]=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{\theta}(a|s)Q^{\pi}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q^{\pi}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q^{\pi}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the immediate reward (correctness) of taking action <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> in state <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>. In our context, since the task is single-turn generation, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q^{\pi}(s,a)\equiv R(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q^{\pi}(s,a)\equiv R(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, predicting the model’s accuracy on a prompt is equivalent to approximating the value function <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{\pi}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{\pi}(s)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>The Monte Carlo Approximation and Pass@1</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Because the action space <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>–encompassing all valid token sequences–is theoretically infinite, calculating the exact expectation <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{\pi}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{\pi}(s)</annotation></semantics></math> is intractable. We therefore employ a Monte Carlo estimator.
For a given prompt <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, we sample <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> independent responses <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math> from the policy <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|s)</annotation></semantics></math> to get <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}(s)</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}(s)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}R(s,a_{i})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}(s)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}R(s,a_{i})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">that <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}(s)</annotation></semantics></math> acts as an approximation of <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{\pi}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{\pi}(s)</annotation></semantics></math>. This <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}(s)</annotation></semantics></math> serves as the ground truth label for our probe. The objective of our probe <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> is to minimize the regression loss over the dataset <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[||\Phi(s,\theta;\phi)-\hat{v}(s)||^{2}\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[||\Phi(s,\theta;\phi)-\hat{v}(s)||^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the learnable parameters of the probe.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The widely used <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Pass}@1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Pass</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Pass}@1</annotation></semantics></math> metric estimates the probability of correctness when sampling one sample from an <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-sample set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>. From the aspect of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Pass}@1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Pass</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Pass}@1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}(s)</annotation></semantics></math> is equivalent to <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Pass}@1(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Pass</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Pass}@1(n)</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is held constant. We can analyze this through the definition of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Pass}@1(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Pass</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Pass}@1(n)</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Pass}@1(n)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}(y_{i}\text{ is correct})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Pass</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> is correct</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Pass}@1(n)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}(y_{i}\text{ is correct})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">which shows the same formulation as <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{v}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{v}(s)</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{I}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{I}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is a decision function). Therefore, modeling <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Pass}@1(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Pass</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Pass}@1(n)</annotation></semantics></math> is equivalent to modeling <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V^{\pi}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V^{\pi}(s)</annotation></semantics></math>. It is worth noting that the commonly used binary metric “accuracy” can be viewed as a special case of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Pass}@1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Pass</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>@</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Pass}@1</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Modeling the Probability of Correctness</h3>

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1 </span>Generative Evaluation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The ability of an LLM to answer a given question relies on two fundamental sources of information: its internal <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">parametric knowledge</span> (<math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>), encapsulated within its network weights, and the <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">contextual knowledge</span> (<math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>) provided by the input prompt <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Petroni et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. The model fuses these two sources to form a high-dimensional latent representation, which we denote as <math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Rep(S,\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Rep(S,\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. Subsequently, a generation function, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>, maps this representation to an answer, and a decision function, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{I}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{I}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>, maps the answer to a binary class that represents correct or incorrect. Therefore, the likelihood <math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> of answering the question correctly can be formulated as:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\mathbb{I}(\psi(Rep(S_{i},\theta))\text{ is correct})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext> is correct</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\mathbb{I}(\psi(Rep(S_{i},\theta))\text{ is correct})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The entire process is computationally expensive due to the sequential nature of the generation process <math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>. It is infeasible for frequent evaluation during model training or for large-scale model selection.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.2 </span>Probe Evaluation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To overcome this efficiency bottleneck, we propose replacing the whole process of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\mathbb{I}(\psi(\cdot))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{n}\sum^{n}_{i=1}\mathbb{I}(\psi(\cdot))</annotation></semantics></math> with a lightweight and efficient <span id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">probe model</span>, denoted as <math id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\cdot;\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\cdot;\phi)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> represents the probe’s parameters. The probe is trained to directly predict the success probability from the LLM’s internal representation:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\approx\hat{p}=f(Rep(S,\theta);\phi)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>≈</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\approx\hat{p}=f(Rep(S,\theta);\phi)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">While this approximation may introduce some level of fidelity loss, it provides a sufficiently reliable estimate for monitoring training dynamics and identifying potential issues, at a fraction of the computational cost. The design of the probe hinges on the choice of the representation <math id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Rep(S,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Rep(S,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> which extracts from the base model. We explore two distinct probe architectures based on different hypotheses about where the most salient information resides.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Probe Architectures</h3>

<section id="S3.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.4.1 </span>Submodel Probe</h4>

<section id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hypothesis 1</h5>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We posit that the model’s parametric knowledge is encoded in the progressive transformation of internal states across layers. Therefore, the probe should have access to the hidden states from various depths of the LLM.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This architecture captures parametric knowledge via the base model’s hidden states. We postulate that the evolution of hidden states across layers forms an ”intrinsic dimension” that correlates with the model’s confidence and capability. Let <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> be the hidden states of the base model <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> at layer <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the sequence length. We construct a lightweight decoder-only probe model with parameters <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>, consisting of <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{probe}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{probe}</annotation></semantics></math> layers. The probe’s input at layer <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> integrates its previous state and the projected hidden state from the base model. Formally, let <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{probe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{probe}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the hidden state of the probe at layer <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>. The update rule is:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z^{(k)}=\text{Decoder}^{(k)}\left(Z^{(k-1)}+W_{proj}^{(k)}H^{(k)};\phi^{(k)}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mtext>Decoder</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z^{(k)}=\text{Decoder}^{(k)}\left(Z^{(k-1)}+W_{proj}^{(k)}H^{(k)};\phi^{(k)}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{proj}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_{probe}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{proj}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_{probe}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a learnable projection matrix, and <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in K</annotation></semantics></math> matches the probe layer index to the corresponding base model layer index (e.g., <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=N</annotation></semantics></math> for a full-layer mapping, or <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K&lt;N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K&lt;N</annotation></semantics></math> for an early-layer mapping, <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of layers in probe, and <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of layers in base model). <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{(k)}=\text{Decoder}^{(k)}(H^{(k-1)};\theta^{(k)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mtext>Decoder</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{(k)}=\text{Decoder}^{(k)}(H^{(k-1)};\theta^{(k)})</annotation></semantics></math> represents the hidden states from base model that contains information from both <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> and <math The final prediction is obtained from the last token representation of the final probe layer <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}=\sigma(\text{Linear}(Z^{(K)}_{[-1]}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>Linear</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}=\sigma(\text{Linear}(Z^{(K)}_{[-1]}))</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z_{[-1]}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z_{[-1]}</annotation></semantics></math> means taking the representation at the last position, and <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is the sigmoid function to bound the output within <math id="S3.SS4.SSS1.Px1.p2.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. The probe model can be formulated as:</p>
