</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.4.2 </span>LoRA Probe</h4>

<section id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hypothesis 2</h5>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that the most direct access to task-specific parametric knowledge is achieved through lightweight perturbations of the frozen model weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This architecture captures parametric knowledge by directly interacting with the weights via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. We interpret the LoRA mechanism not just as fine-tuning, but as a probe that modulates the frozen parametric knowledge <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> based on contextual knowledge <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>.
If we treat the LoRA module <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="AB" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">AB</annotation></semantics></math> as the probe model’s weight <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>, the standard LoRA formulation can be rewritten as:</p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y=(W_{\theta}+AB)X=W_{\phi}X+W_{\theta}X" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y=(W_{\theta}+AB)X=W_{\phi}X+W_{\theta}X</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">therefore the probe model takes both <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\in S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\in S</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\theta}\in\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\theta}\in\theta</annotation></semantics></math> as inputs through the following formulation:</p>
<table id="S3.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}f_{lora}(Rep(S,\theta);\phi)=&amp;\tilde{D}^{(n)}\circ\tilde{D}^{(n-1)}\circ\dots\\
&amp;\circ\tilde{D}^{(1)}(H^{(1)};\theta,\phi)\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}f_{lora}(Rep(S,\theta);\phi)=&amp;\tilde{D}^{(n)}\circ\tilde{D}^{(n-1)}\circ\dots\\
&amp;\circ\tilde{D}^{(1)}(H^{(1)};\theta,\phi)\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{D}(H;\theta,\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{D}(H;\theta,\phi)</annotation></semantics></math> is a standard decoder layer operated by LoRA through <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{W}=W_{\theta}+AB" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{W}=W_{\theta}+AB</annotation></semantics></math>. We attach LoRA adapters <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi=\{A_{l},B_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi=\{A_{l},B_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> to the base model. Unlike standard LoRA for text generation, we optimize these adapters solely for the regression task:</p>
<table id="S3.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}=\sigma(\text{Linear}(f_{lora}(Rep(S,\theta);\phi)_{[-1]}))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>Linear</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}=\sigma(\text{Linear}(f_{lora}(Rep(S,\theta);\phi)_{[-1]}))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.4" class="ltx_p">This architecture implicitly learns to measure the “competence” of the base model weights <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> for the given input <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> by learning the necessary correction <math id="S3.SS4.SSS2.Px1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> required to map the state to its value estimate.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>In-Training Probe Evaluation Pipeline</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The in-training probe evaluation pipeline requires an initial probe training phase, after which the trained probe can be utilized to evaluate future checkpoints.
Consider a set of downstream tasks, each containing a training set and a test set (or manually split it if necessary). The pipeline proceeds as follows:</p>
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Data Collection: Perform a generative evaluation on the training set to compute the probability of correctness (i.e., Pass@1), which is assigned as the label for each prompt.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Probe Training: Formulate the problem as a regression task, using the prompt as input and the calculated probability as the training target.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Probe Evaluation: Feed prompts from the test set into the probe to predict the probability of correctness.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.2" class="ltx_p">In terms of computational cost, phase 1 and 2 are the most intensive. However, once a probe is trained, it can predict the Pass@1 value using a single forward pass, significantly accelerating the evaluation process at phase 3.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we empirically validate the effectiveness of the proposed In-Training Probe Evaluation framework. We aim to scrutinize the framework’s capability to monitor downstream performance efficiently and accurately throughout the LLM training lifecycle. Specifically, our experiments are designed to address the following research questions:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ1 (Fidelity):</span> Can lightweight probes accurately approximate the downstream performance of LLMs solely based on internal representations?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ2 (Generalizability):</span> Do probes trained on early checkpoints exhibit transferability to future checkpoints, despite the significant distribution shifts incurred during training?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ3 (Efficiency):</span> What is the magnitude of computational acceleration achieved by our framework compared to traditional generative evaluation paradigms?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets Preparation.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">o ensure a comprehensive assessment of model capabilities, we curate a diverse benchmark suite spanning three primary domains:
(1) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reasoning</span>: We employ GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, MATH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>, AIME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Veeraboina, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Math-AI, 2025</a>)</cite> to evaluate mathematical problem-solving, GPQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rein et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for graduate-level scientific reasoning, and BBH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2022a</a>)</cite> for symbolic reasoning tasks.
(2) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Knowledge</span>: The MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021a</a>)</cite> benchmark is utilized to assess massive multitask language understanding.
(3) <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coding</span>: We adopt HumanEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021a</a>)</cite> and MBPP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al., 2021</a>)</cite> to evaluate code generation proficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each dataset, we construct the training targets by performing a standard generative evaluation. Specifically, we define the ground truth label as the empirical success probability, estimated by sampling <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> responses per prompt (denoted as Pass@1(<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>)). Detailed statistics and configuration of the datasets are summarized in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In Datasets Preparation. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Data Preparation ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Summary of datasets used for probe training and evaluation. <span id="S4.T1.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">N-shot</span> denotes the number of in-context exemplars. <span id="S4.T1.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage</span> indicates the applicable training phase: <span id="S4.T1.9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Pre</span> (Pre-training) and <span id="S4.T1.9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Post</span> (Post-training/Instruction Tuning). <span id="S4.T1.9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sampling Budget (<math id="S4.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>)</span> refers to the number of samples generated to estimate the ground-truth Pass@1 score in pre/post stage.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Base Models and Checkpoints.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct our experiments using the OLMo3-7B’s checkpoints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olmo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, because of its open accessibility to granular checkpoints across the training trajectory. To rigorously evaluate the robustness of our probes against distribution shifts, we utilize a sequence of checkpoints spanning two distinct training phases:</p>
<ol id="S4.I2" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pre-training Phase:</span> We sample intermediate checkpoints at varying step intervals during the fundamental language modeling stage (i.e., OLMo-3-1025-7B<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                    <a href="https://huggingface.co/allenai/Olmo-3-1025-7B" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/allenai/Olmo-3-1025-7B</a></span></span></span>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Post-training Phase:</span> We include checkpoints from instruction tuning and alignment stages (i.e., OLMo-3-7B-Instruct<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                    <a href="https://huggingface.co/allenai/Olmo-3-7B-Instruct" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/allenai/Olmo-3-7B-Instruct</a></span></span></span> and OLMo-3-7B-Think<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                      <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                      
                    <a href="https://huggingface.co/allenai/Olmo-3-7B-Think" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/allenai/Olmo-3-7B-Think</a></span></span></span>).</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To benchmark the effectiveness of our proposed architectures, we compare them against
two established baselines: 1. <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Loss fit</span>, a conventional metric that uses the negative log-likelihood to predict the value. This baseline assumes that lower perplexity correlates with higher downstream accuracy. 2. <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Linear probe</span>, a simplified version of our framework, where each layer trained a linear regressor to predict the final value. This serves to isolate the gains attributed to our proposed non-linear probe architectures (Submodel and LoRA). See Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Baselines ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for more implementation details. We also provide a comparison with subset sampling in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Comparison with Subset Sampling ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation Metrics.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The probes are trained to regress the success probability <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}</annotation></semantics></math>. To quantify the estimation quality, we applied a binary classification process to the Pass@1 value in metrics computation: We binarized the ground truth Pass@1 values using a threshold of 0.5, i.e., <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=\mathbb{I}(\text{Pass@1}\geq 0.5)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝕀</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>Pass@1</mtext><mo>≥</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=\mathbb{I}(\text{Pass@1}\geq 0.5)</annotation></semantics></math> and report the <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC)</span>. AUROC is threshold-independent and robust to class imbalance, making it an ideal metric to measure how well the probe’s predicted scores rank successful instances higher than failed ones. A larger AUROC value means better probe performance: <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AUROC}=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>AUROC</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AUROC}=1.0</annotation></semantics></math> indicates perfect prediction; <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AUROC}=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>AUROC</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AUROC}=0.5</annotation></semantics></math> indicates random guessing. Additionally, we also reported Mean Squared Error (MSE) <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lVert\hat{p}-p\rVert_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>−</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lVert\hat{p}-p\rVert_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> as an evidence for goodness of fit.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>RQ1: High-Fidelity Performance Estimation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first assess the fundamental capability of the proposed probes to approximate ground-truth performance metrics (Pass@1) using only internal representations. <a href="#S4.T2" title="In Datasets Preparation. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents the comparative results on the pre-training checkpoints.
The Loss Fit baseline yields an average AUROC of only 0.5795, barely outperforming random guessing (0.5). This corroborates the “emergence” phenomenon in LLMs, where training loss cannot correctly correlate with the ability to solve complex reasoning tasks. Similarly, the Linear probe fails to extract sufficient signals (Avg. AUROC of 0.5810), suggesting that the mapping from static representations to task success is highly non-linear.
The proposed Submodel architecture significantly outperforms all baselines, achieving an average AUROC of 0.7890 and reducing MSE to 0.1049. From these results, we can conclude that Submodel is sufficient to approximate the correctness with high relevance and low error.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Notably, probes on tasks like HumanEval and BBH can achieve higher AUROCs compared to other tasks, while MMLU is less predictable. The discussion and more related information are in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Full Results ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>, where we demonstrate all results in the pre-training and post-training stages.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>RQ2: Cross-Checkpoint Generalizability</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A critical requirement for in-training monitoring is <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Forward Transferability</span>: can a probe trained on an earlier checkpoint (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>) accurately forecast the performance of a future checkpoint (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t+\Delta t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+\Delta t</annotation></semantics></math>)? We investigate this by training probes on specific checkpoints (rows in <a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.3 RQ2: Cross-Checkpoint Generalizability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) and testing them on subsequent checkpoints (columns).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.3 RQ2: Cross-Checkpoint Generalizability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the Submodel probe demonstrates exceptional temporal robustness. For instance, a probe trained at step 200k maintains an AUROC of <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 0.75</annotation></semantics></math> even when evaluated on the final checkpoint (Last), despite massive updates to the base model’s weights. This implies that the mapping between hidden state dynamics and task correctness is an <em id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">invariant property</em> of the model architecture, independent of specific weight values.
Conversely, the LoRA probe suffers from significant degradation when transferred to future checkpoints (e.g., dropping from 0.67 to 0.56). This confirms our hypothesis: LoRA learns to modulate specific weight matrices (<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>), and as <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> drifts during training, the learned modulation <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta W_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta W_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> becomes obsolete. In contrast, the Submodel operates on the <em id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">semantic representation space</em>, which evolves more smoothly.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.T3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Forward Transferability Analysis.<span id="S4.T3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We report AUROC scores where probes are trained on earlier checkpoints (rows) and tested on future checkpoints (columns).</span></span></figcaption>

<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>RQ3: Computational Efficiency and Amortized Cost</h3>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2604.01025v1/base_time.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:429/357;" width="429" height="357"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cumulative time consumption for Probe Evaluation vs. Generative Evaluation on pre-training checkpoints (OLMo-3-Base).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the accuracy and generalizability have been demonstrated, another core focus of the proposed framework is efficiency, that is, whether it can replace traditional generative evaluation to achieve low-latency assessment.
We analyze the computational cost of the probe evaluation pipeline compared to standard generative evaluation. The total time cost <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> can be modeled as <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=T_{init}+N\times t_{eval}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=T_{init}+N\times t_{eval}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of evaluations. Generative evaluation does not contain a <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{init}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{init}</annotation></semantics></math>, however, it usually contains a high <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{eval}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{eval}</annotation></semantics></math>. While probe evaluation requires a preparation phase, its <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{eval}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{eval}</annotation></semantics></math> is significantly smaller than generative evaluation.
As illustrated in <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4.4 RQ3: Computational Efficiency and Amortized Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, although the probe method requires an initialization phase (data collection + training), it achieves a <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">15.6<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup</span> in inference per checkpoint on the base model–while generative evaluation requires 0.78h to finish an evaluation, probe evaluation only takes 0.05h. The advantage becomes even more pronounced in post-training stages where generation length increases. As detailed in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Time Comparison ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>, the speedup factors reach <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">61.4<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math></span> for instruct models and <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">231.8<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math></span> for think models. This makes our framework particularly suitable for high-frequency monitoring of modern reasoning models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Ablation: Layer-wise Information Sufficiency</h3>

<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.T4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Impact of Input Layer Depth.<span id="S4.T4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Comparison of Submodel probes trained on the first <math id="S4.T4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> layers versus the full model (32 layers).</span></span></figcaption>
<table id="S4.T4.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T4.6.1" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S4.T4.6.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.6079</td>
<td id="S4.T4.6.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.6663</td>
<td id="S4.T4.6.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.6921</td>

<td id="S4.T4.6.4.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">0.7822</td>
<td id="S4.T4.6.4.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">0.7890</td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we investigate the minimal information required for accurate prediction. The Submodel probe normally aggregates hidden states from all layers. Here, we analyze the performance impact of restricting the input to the first <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> layers (“Early Exit” strategy).
<a href="#S4.T4" title="In 4.5 Ablation: Layer-wise Information Sufficiency ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reveals that the first 16 layers contain the majority of the signal required for performance estimation (Avg. AUROC 0.7725 vs. 0.7890). However, reducing the scope to only the first 8 layers results in a notable performance drop, indicating that critical reasoning cues are distributed across the mid-to-upper layers of the network. This finding supports the feasibility of further accelerating the pipeline by caching only the upper-layer representations.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we address the critical bottleneck of efficiently monitoring the downstream performance of LLMs during training, where the imperative for frequent monitoring conflicts with the computationally prohibitive cost of standard generative benchmarks. We introduce the In-Training <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Probe Evaluation</span> framework, a novel paradigm that substitutes the high latency generative evaluation paradigm with agile, efficient diagnostic probes. By formulating performance estimation as a value approximation problem, we demonstrate that lightweight probes can accurately regress the probabilities of correctness on downstream tasks from the model’s internal representations, bypassing the need for full-scale generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our extensive experiments yield two pivotal insights. First, we establish that the correlation between internal hidden states and task correctness is remarkably invariant to the distribution shifts inherent in model training. Specifically, our Submodel probe architecture exhibits strong <span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">forward transferability</span>: a probe trained on previous checkpoints can reliably forecast the performance of future checkpoints. Second, we quantify the efficiency gains, demonstrating that our framework reduces evaluation latency by orders of magnitude (<math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="15.6\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>15.6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15.6\times</annotation></semantics></math> speed up compared with generative evaluation), rendering high-frequency, granular monitoring feasible once again.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Looking ahead, this work lays the foundation for a more controllable and scientifically grounded LLM development process. The implications extend beyond passive monitoring; our framework offers a viable path toward active training intervention. The high-fidelity signals provided by these probes could serve as real-time feedback mechanisms for dynamic data curriculum learning—allowing developers to adjust data mixtures or hyperparameters on-the-fly to optimize specific downstream capabilities. By decoupling evaluation costs from model scale, we provide a scalable methodology to accelerate the iteration and understanding of next-generation AI systems.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Large Language Models In-Training Supervision. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Data Preparation</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Preparation Process</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Data preparation requires splitting datasets into training and test sets. For MMLU and GSM8k, which already contain standard splits, we use them directly. However, other datasets do not provide a training split; therefore, we manually perform a train-test split for BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, and GPQA. Specifically, for MATH, we use MATH-500 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lightman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> as the test set and the original MATH dataset (excluding MATH-500) as the training set. For BBH, which consists of multiple subsets, we select 50 samples from each subset for the test set and use the remaining data for training. Finally, we randomly downsample the training sets of MMLU and MATH, as their large size would make the evaluation time cost prohibitive.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>MMLU Prompt Format</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Think step by step and answer the following questions. 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Question: {question} 
<br class="ltx_break">(A) {option 1} (B) {option 2} (C) {option 3} (D) {option 4} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Answer: {answer} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">{the rest 4 shots} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Question: {question} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Answer: Let’s think step by step.
</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>GSM8K Prompt Format</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Question: {question} 
<br class="ltx_break">Answer: {chain-of-thought} 
<br class="ltx_break">### {answer} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">{the rest 7 shots} 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">Question: {question} 
<br class="ltx_break">Answer:
</span></p>
</div>
</section>

<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.

<br class="ltx_break">Answer:
</span></p>

</section>

<section id="A1.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.7 </span>AIME Prompt Format</h3>

<div id="A1.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">{question}
</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.8 </span>GPQA Prompt Format</h3>

<div id="A1.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.

</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Baselines</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Linear Probe</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Linear Probe shares the same paradigm as the proposed probing methods. It collects hidden states from the base model and applies linear regression to each layer to obtain a predicted value. The average of these predicted values is then used to estimate the probability of correctness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Loss Curve Fit</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2025)</a></cite>, who utilized regression to link loss values to downstream performance, we model the relationship between the model’s loss on a given input and its final probability of correctness. Specifically, we collect loss values and the corresponding correctness probabilities for all prompts and perform linear regression using ordinary least squares. To predict downstream performance, we input the loss of a given prompt into the trained regression model to estimate its probability of correctness.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Full Results</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the full results on each dataset for checkpoints from the pre-training stage (base model) and the post-training stage (instruct and think).</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">

</section>
<section id="A3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.4 </span>Discussion on Performance</h3>

<div id="A3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing across datasets, HumanEval, BBH, MATH and MBPP are relatively easy to predict, while MMLU, AIME and GPQA are hard.
AIME and GPQA are extremely hard benchmarks that require ultra long reasoning steps to provide the correct answer. Contrary to our initial expectations of poor performance, we were surprised to find that the probe exhibited meaningful predictive capability on these two datasets. Specifically, it generally achieved scores above 0.6 on both instruct model and think model, and even surpassed 0.75 on AIME in instruct model. This suggests a possibility that, with further research, datasets like AIME, which typically require tens of thousands of tokens for evaluation, could be assessed without generation, relying solely on the internal states elicited by the input prompt to predict correctness.
For MMLU, we attribute the subpar performance to insufficient training data. Although the full MMLU training set contains nearly 100k samples, we utilized only 10k (concerning the generation time). This sample size is relatively small compared to the <math id="A3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>14k test samples, preventing the probe from fully capturing the dataset’s features and ultimately resulting in mediocre predictive capability.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Comparison with Subset Sampling</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Subset sampling is an efficient evaluation method commonly used in industry. It approximates an LLM’s performance on a full dataset by evaluating it on a smaller subset. The comparison between probes and subset sampling primarily focuses on two aspects: 1. If both methods are constrained to the same level of efficiency, which one provides a more accurate assessment of the model’s performance on the full dataset? 2. Without excessive efficiency constraints, can the probe method maintain its performance on the sampled subset, thereby consistently achieving higher efficiency than the subset approach?</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For aspect 1, we constrain the number of evaluation steps to 50 iters. Therefore, to match the probe’s efficiency, the time cost of subset sampling is <math id="A4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\times T_{subset}=T_{init}+50\times{t_{e}val}\geq T_{init}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\times T_{subset}=T_{init}+50\times{t_{e}val}\geq T_{init}</annotation></semantics></math>, as <math id="A4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{eval}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{eval}</annotation></semantics></math> is negligible. Then, we can get that <math id="A4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{subset}=\frac{T_{init}}{50}=\frac{T_{fullset}+T_{train}}{50}\geq\frac{T_{fullset}}{50}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mn>50</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mn>50</mn></mfrac><mo>≥</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mn>50</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{subset}=\frac{T_{init}}{50}=\frac{T_{fullset}+T_{train}}{50}\geq\frac{T_{fullset}}{50}</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, we set 2% as the proportion of subset size. The evaluation results are shown in <a href="#A4.T8" title="In Appendix D Comparison with Subset Sampling ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. It demonstrates that compared with subset sampling, probe evaluation obtains an overall smaller absolute error in assessing the performance on the full dataset.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T8" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A4.T8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 8</span>: </span><span id="A4.T8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison between probe evaluation and subset sampling on absolute error (smaller is better).</span></figcaption>
<table id="A4.T8.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A4.T8.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A4.T8.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">Absolute Error</td>
<td id="A4.T8.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">HumanEval</td>
<td id="A4.T8.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">MATH</td>
<td id="A4.T8.5.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">BBH</td>
<td id="A4.T8.5.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">MMLU</td>
<td id="A4.T8.5.1.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">GSM8k</td>
<td id="A4.T8.5.1.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt">MBPP</td></tr>
<tr id="A4.T8.5.2" class="ltx_tr">

</figure>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For aspect 2, we set the subset size to 20%, and conduct a probe evaluation on the subset. <a href="#A4.T9" title="In Appendix D Comparison with Subset Sampling ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> shows the comparison between probe trained on subset and trained on fullset. It demonstrates that even when the subset size is reduced to 20%, the probe’s performance on the subset remains close to its performance on the fullset, with only a slight and minor decline.</p>
</div>

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Time Comparison</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the time costs for the two models in the post-training stage (Instruct and Think). For the Instruct model, probe evaluation achieves a 61.4x speedup compared to generative evaluation, with its amortized time cost falling below that of generative evaluation after 11 evaluation steps. For the Think model, the efficiency gain reaches 231.8x, becoming more cost-effective than generative evaluation after just 9 evaluation steps.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A5.F4.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2604.01025v1/instruction_time.svg" id="A5.F4.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/397;" width="476" height="397"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F4.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="A5.F4.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">OLMo-3-7B-Instruct</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A5.F4.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2604.01025v1/think_time.svg" id="A5.F4.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/397;" width="476" height="397"></object>

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="A5.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cumulative time consumption for Probe Evaluation vs. Generative Evaluation on post-training checkpoints for Instruct and Think models.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The probe preparation time includes the data collection time (i.e., conduct a generative evaluation on trainset) and the probe training time, as indicated by the y-axis intercept of the “probe evaluation” line in <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4.4 RQ3: Computational Efficiency and Amortized Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#A5.F4" title="In Appendix E Time Comparison ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. The specific time values are presented in <a href="#A5.T10" title="In Appendix E Time Comparison ‣ Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs’ Downstream Performances" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Discussion on Data Selection</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Another discussion concerns the selection of training data. To ensure experimental rigor in this study, we maintained a strict separation between training and test sets, ensuring the test data remained unseen during the probe’s training. This setup implicitly tests the probe’s ability to generalize from training samples to test samples. However, in real-world industrial scenarios, this type of generalization is not strictly necessary. In practice, the primary objective is to accurately model the mapping from input data to downstream metrics; overfitting to the specific dataset is acceptable, provided that cross-checkpoint generalization is preserved. Consequently, practical applications can forgo the train/test split and train the probe directly on the target evaluation set. This approach would yield higher monitoring accuracy and further reduce the time overhead of the probe preparation phase.</p>
</div>
</section>
